The market opened at dawn, and dawn was generous that morning, spilling a lavish apricot light across the stalls and the faces of the vendors who had arrived in darkness. Oranges were stacked in pyramids of impossible geometry. Fish lay on ice with the dignified stillness of the recently deceased. A woman sold bread that smelled of another century... of woodsmoke and patience and the slow alchemy of yeast. He wandered through the aisles like a pilgrim in a cathedral built of commerce. The voices rose around him, a canopy of languages he could not parse but understood in the way one understands music... through rhythm, through feeling, through the architecture of sound. He bought plums. They were heavy in his palm, purple as bruises, sweet as the first hour of sleep. He ate one standing in the sun, and the juice ran down his wrist, and he thought... this is enough. This single plum. This borrowed morning. Enough.
